# Preface {.unnumbered}

This report describes snapy as the code implements it: for each scheme, what it does, where it comes from, how
it is discretized, where it lives in the code, how it is tested and where it stops working. Every statement is
derived on the page, cited to the code at a pinned commit, or cited to a test with its tolerance.

## Pins {.unnumbered}

Code is cited by file and symbol, resolved at one pinned commit of
[`chengcli/snapy`](https://github.com/chengcli/snapy). That commit is recorded in `doc/tech-report/code_pin.yml`
and printed in the build note below for readers of the PDF. Every code citation identifies a file and, where applicable, a symbol at that pinned commit.

## Install and run {#sec-preface-install .unnumbered}

Every input file, switch and command in this book is written for snapy at the pin above, built from source. The
releases on PyPI (`pip install snapy`) are older than the pin. They lack the environment switches of chapters 4 to
6 (`SNAP_WB_REF4`, `SNAP_X1_CENTROID_EXACT`, `SNAP_X1_MASS_COVARIANCE`, `SNAP_GRAVITY_WORK_RADIAL_EXACT`), and a
switch the code does not know is ignored without a message. Older releases also refuse the `gravity-work` keys of
chapter 6. So build the pin, as below, before you try any example.

<!-- generated reader-reference: install -->
**What you need.** Python `>=3.10` ([`pyproject.toml:24`](https://github.com/chengcli/snapy/blob/919936da07d80a310b98ab11da184972a3203274/pyproject.toml#L24)), CMake 3.22 or later ([`CMakeLists.txt:1`](https://github.com/chengcli/snapy/blob/919936da07d80a310b98ab11da184972a3203274/CMakeLists.txt#L1)), a C++17 compiler ([`CMakeLists.txt:3`](https://github.com/chengcli/snapy/blob/919936da07d80a310b98ab11da184972a3203274/CMakeLists.txt#L3)), and the NetCDF C library. Install the latter with `brew install netcdf` on macOS or `sudo apt install libnetcdf-dev` on Debian/Ubuntu.

**Build the source pin.** The Python dependencies below follow [`pyproject.toml`](https://github.com/chengcli/snapy/blob/919936da07d80a310b98ab11da184972a3203274/pyproject.toml); the CMake options explicitly enable the example drivers and disable the optional UCX and parallel-NetCDF backends for this single-machine build.

```bash
python3 -m venv snapy-env && source snapy-env/bin/activate
pip install numpy pyyaml "kintera>=2.6.3" torch==2.10.0
git clone https://github.com/chengcli/snapy && cd snapy
git checkout 919936da07d80a310b98ab11da184972a3203274
cmake -B build -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release \
  -DBUILD_EXAMPLES=ON -DNETCDF=ON -DPNETCDF=OFF -DUCX=OFF
cmake --build build --parallel 6
pip install .
```
<!-- end reader-reference: install -->

`-DUCX=OFF` builds the Gloo backend only, which is all a single machine needs; @sec-ch14-backends describes UCX.
The build also compiles the tests (`BUILD_TESTS` is on by default). A test named in a Tests layer runs with
`ctest --test-dir build -R <name>`; to reproduce a documented test case and check it against the book, follow
@sec-ch15-metrics. The last line installs the Python package from the same build, which the Python
listings of the chapters import (`import snapy`), and puts the tools `pd-run`, `pd-combine` and `pd-inspect` on
the path.

**Run a deck.** The build puts one driver program per example in `build/bin`, next to links to the decks of
`examples/`. A deck is a YAML input file, and a *driver* is the program that reads it, sets the initial state
and steps the model ({{< code examples/straka.cpp ParseArguments >}},
{{< code src/mesh/meshblock_options.cpp MeshBlockOptionsImpl::from_yaml >}}). See @sec-ch01-initialization
for the distinction between a deck, a case and a restart file. The Straka cold bubble runs on one process with

```bash
cd build/bin
./straka.release straka_single.yaml
```

It prints one line per ten cycles and stops at 900 s of model time, after about 3700 cycles (half a minute on six
CPU cores). It writes `straka_single.out0.00000.nc` and `straka_single.out0.00001.nc`, the start and the end state.
A deck split into several blocks runs on several processes, launched with `torchrun`. The number of processes $N$
is the number of blocks divided by `blocks_per_process`. `straka_proc2.yaml` has two blocks along $x_2$ and one
block per process, so $N = 2$ (about 20 s):

```bash
torchrun --no-python --nproc-per-node=2 --master-port=29573 ./straka.release straka_proc2.yaml
```

Pick any free port for `--master-port` (@sec-ch14-launch). A process count that does not match the deck stops at
construction with "world_size (1) does not match layout partitioning (2)".

The 2-D warm-bubble test is `bryan.yaml`, a moist warm bubble on one block ($x_1$ by $x_2$, 200 by 400 cells): its
`problem` card sets the bubble's amplitude `dT`, centre `xc`, `zc` and radii `xr`, `zr`. It runs the same way,
`./bryan.release bryan.yaml`, stops at 1000 s of model time and writes one output frame every 100 s.

**The same example on one GPU.** Rebuild with the `CUDA` option on
([`CMakeLists.txt:10`](https://github.com/chengcli/snapy/blob/919936da07d80a310b98ab11da184972a3203274/CMakeLists.txt#L10)),
that is, with `-DCUDA=ON` added to the build command above, then select the device with two environment variables:

```bash
cd build/bin
DEVICE=cuda DEVICE_ID=0 ./straka.release straka_single.yaml
```

`DEVICE` defaults to `cpu`
([`src/layout/layout.cpp:238`](https://github.com/chengcli/snapy/blob/919936da07d80a310b98ab11da184972a3203274/src/layout/layout.cpp#L238));
with `cuda`, the block runs on `cuda:<DEVICE_ID>`, or on the local rank's GPU when `DEVICE_ID` is unset
({{< code src/mesh/meshblock_options.cpp MeshBlockOptionsImpl::device_str >}}).
The driver prints "Running on CUDA" before the first step when it got a GPU
(`main` of {{< code examples/straka.cpp main >}});
without that line it is running on the CPU. @sec-ch14-gpu covers the rest of GPU execution.

**Which driver for which deck.** `straka.release` runs dry Cartesian decks such as `straka_single.yaml`;
`bryan.release` runs the moist `bryan.yaml`; `run_hydro.release -i <deck>` needs a deck with a `reactions:` card,
such as `jupiter_evap_precip_1d.yaml`, and stops on a dry deck. A "minimal input" in a chapter is a fragment, not
a deck: add its keys to a copy of a complete deck (`straka_single.yaml` for a dry run, `bryan.yaml` for a moist
one) and run that copy. An environment switch goes in front of the driver, as in
`SNAP_WB_REF4=1 ./straka.release deck.yaml`.
